title: Inversions / possessives
subtitle: Negative adverbial inversions, so / neither, and possessive forms

theory.title: Inversions with negative adverbial words and phrases

blocks.text: When we put some negative adverbial words and phrases at the beginning of a sentence for emphasis, the subject and the verb 'invert'. This means we use the question form of the verb, even though the sentence is not a question. Inversions are quite formal and are not usually used in conversation.

blocks.intro: Form: negative adverbial word/phrase + question form
items: **No sooner had I** accepted the job than they told me I had to work weekends.

rows.example: **Never have I worked** so hard in all my life.
**Rarely have I worked** so hard in all my life.
**Seldom have I worked** so hard in all my life.
**No sooner had Matt started** work than he resigned.
**Hardly had Matt started** work when he resigned.
**Not only were you** late for work, but you had **also** forgotten the report.
**Under no circumstances are employees allowed** to leave the building without permission.
**At no time / point was I told** what the job involved.
**Little did I realise** that I would become managing director just two years later.
**Not until the next day did I hear** that I had got the job.
**Only at the end of the interview did I think** I had a chance of getting the job.

blocks.text: **Little** is used with verbs of thought (**realise**, **know**, **suspect**, etc.) and means 'I did not realise / etc. at all…'.

items: **Little did I know** how things were going to turn out. (= I did not know at all how things were going to turn out.)

blocks.text: With **not until** and **only**, you have to be careful about which verb to invert. Invert the verb in the **main** clause, not in the time clause.

blocks.correct: **Not until I had finished** my homework **was I allowed** to go out.
blocks.incorrect: Not until had I finished my homework I was allowed to go out.

blocks.correct: **Only when I had finished** my homework **was I allowed** to go out.
blocks.incorrect: Only when had I finished my homework I was allowed to go out.

rows.use: In short answers and other similar structures using so, neither and nor
rows.example: 'I'm a plumber.' 'Really? **So am I**!' My sister doesn't like getting ready for work, and **neither do I / nor do I**.
The manager was nervous about the director's visit, **as were the rest of the staff**. **So late was it** that there was no one in the office. **Such a hot day was it** that no one wanted to work.
**Were our staff** better trained, we might make a larger profit. (= If our staff were better trained …) **Had I known** about the vacancy, I would have applied. (= If I had known …)

blocks.text: Remember that **So am/do/have I** is used to agree with a positive statement and **Neither/Nor am/do/have I** is used to agree with a negative statement.

blocks.correct: 'I really like my job.' '**So do I.**'
blocks.incorrect: I really like my job. Neither do I.

blocks.correct: 'I really don't like my job.' '**Neither do I / Nor do I.**'
blocks.incorrect: I really don't like my job. So do I.

blocks.text: We can show possession by using **'s** and **s'**.

rows.use: 's with singular nouns, including names, and with irregular plurals which do not end in -s
rows.example: That's the **manager's** car, over there. We are still waiting for **Sarah's** decision about who to take on. I think that **women's** rights should be protected by law.

rows.use: just an apostrophe with regular plural nouns ending in -s
rows.example: The **workers'** pay was increased by ten percent.

rows.use: 's or s' in some time expressions
rows.example: After an **hour's** wait, I finally got to see the manager. I'll be at the factory in about **ten minutes'** time.

rows.use: 's or s' with people (or groups composed of people) and animals; the/my/etc. for other things
rows.example: Is this **John's** briefcase? We held a meeting to discuss the **company's** finances. The vet had a close look at the **cat's** paw. The technician had a close look at the back of **my** computer. (not … at my computer's back)

blocks.text: With singular names ending in **-s**, some people use **'s** and some people just add an apostrophe. They are both correct, although using **'s** is more common.

items: The report is on **Charles's** computer in the office.
The report is on **Charles'** computer in the office.

blocks.text: With plural names ending in **-s**, we just add an apostrophe, as with other plurals.
With phrases, the possessive **'s** and **s'** must go at the end of the whole phrase.

blocks.correct: **Tom, Dick and Harry's** office is around here somewhere.
blocks.incorrect: Tom's, Dick's and Harry's office is around here somewhere.

blocks.correct: The **President of France's** visit to England will be good for business.
blocks.incorrect: The President's of France visit to England will be good for business.

rows.use: Possessive determiners (my, your, his, her, its, our, their) come before a noun and show possession
rows.example: I'm really excited about **my** new job. Are you looking forward to meeting **your** new boss?

rows.use: Possessive pronouns (mine, yours, his, hers, ours, yours, theirs) are used instead of a noun
rows.example: My new job is great. How about **yours**? (= …your job) Our business is doing quite well, but I hear Simon and Julie are having problems with **theirs**. (= …their business)

rows.use: Possessive pronouns can also be used after of to show possession
rows.example: She's a colleague **of mine**. (= …one of my colleagues) Are they customers **of yours**?

blocks.text: A common mistake to be avoided is using a possessive pronoun instead of a possessive determiner or using a possessive determiner instead of a pronoun.

blocks.correct: I don't really get on so well with **my** boss.
blocks.incorrect: I don't really get on so well with mine boss.

blocks.correct: I know your job is dangerous, but did Frank and Jenny tell you about **theirs**?
blocks.incorrect: I know your job is dangerous, but did Frank and Jenny tell you about their?

blocks.text: Remember that there are no apostrophes in possessive pronouns.

blocks.correct: I know your job is dangerous, but did Frank and Jenny tell you about **theirs**?
blocks.incorrect: I know your job is dangerous, but did Frank and Jenny tell you about their's?

blocks.text: Don't get confused between **its** (possessive determiner, without an apostrophe) and **it's** (contraction for **it is** or **it has**, with an apostrophe).

blocks.correct: Our company is hoping to increase **its** share of the market.
blocks.incorrect: Our company is hoping to increase it's share of the market.

exercises.title: C · Correct the inversion
exercises.instruction: If the word or phrase in bold is correct, write it again. If it is incorrect, rewrite it correctly.

items.prompt: Hardly **Tom had** opened the door when the dog ran out into the street.
Only when I **read** the book did I realise why it was so special.
Not only **you passed** the exam, but you also got an A!
Not until **do I see** Greg next week will I know whether he got the job.
No sooner **had we found** our seats than the film began.
At no point while the race is taking place **members of the public are not allowed** onto the track.

exercises.title: E · Keep the meaning
exercises.instruction: Complete the sentences so that the meaning remains the same.

items.prompt:
Photographs are not permitted under any circumstances.
**Under**
acceptedAnswers: Under no circumstances are photographs permitted.
Under no circumstances are photographs allowed.

items.prompt:
We've never faced such a serious problem as this.
**Never**
acceptedAnswers: Never have we faced such a serious problem as this.
Never have we faced such a serious problem.

items.prompt:
I only realised it was Vanessa when she removed her hat.
**Only**
acceptedAnswers: Only when she removed her hat did I realise it was Vanessa.
Only when she removed her hat did I realize it was Vanessa.

items.prompt:
The audience didn't laugh at any point during the show.
**At**
acceptedAnswers: At no point during the show did the audience laugh.
At no point did the audience laugh during the show.

items.prompt:
As soon as Patrick had finished the e-mail, he sent it.
**No**
acceptedAnswers: No sooner had Patrick finished the e-mail than he sent it.
No sooner had Patrick finished the email than he sent it.

items.prompt:
It wasn't clear who was going to win the match until the last few minutes.
**Not**
acceptedAnswers: Not until the last few minutes was it clear who was going to win the match.
Not until the last few minutes was it clear who would win the match.

items.prompt:
Dennis passed his driving test and had an accident almost immediately afterwards.
**Hardly**
acceptedAnswers: Hardly had Dennis passed his driving test when he had an accident.
Hardly had Dennis passed his driving test when he had an accident almost immediately afterwards.

items.prompt:
I didn't learn the result of the match until I read the evening paper.
**Only**
acceptedAnswers: Only when I read the evening paper did I learn the result of the match.
Only after I read the evening paper did I learn the result of the match.

items.prompt:
The president will not resign under any circumstances.
**Under**
acceptedAnswers: Under no circumstances will the president resign.
Under no circumstances will the president resign

items.prompt:
The accused showed no emotion at any time during the trial.
**At**
acceptedAnswers: At no time during the trial did the accused show any emotion.
At no time during the trial did the accused show emotion.
